title: Listening and putting it together
summary: Train your ear on what you have learned, then work out a real song: its key, its numbers and its groove. Project: learn a song by theory.

lessons.title: Ear training you can do every day

videos.title: Major or minor chords? Ear training game (CSound)

practice.question: You're using the major-or-minor ear training video. What makes it actual practice rather than just watching?
options: Letting the answers play and nodding along
Only watching the chords you got right last time
Watching it at double speed
Saying your answer out loud before each reveal and keeping your own score
practice.explanation: The video can't hear you or keep score: it's guided listening, not an assessment. It only trains your ear if you commit to an answer first and track your own ticks and crosses.

practice.question: C major is C E G. Which note changes to make C minor?
options: C becomes C#
E becomes Eb
G becomes Gb
G becomes G#
practice.explanation: Only the middle note (the third) drops a half step: C Eb G. Major is 4 + 3 half steps; minor is 3 + 4.

practice.question: Which practice plan will train your ear fastest?
options: Five to ten minutes every day, one skill at a time
One hour once a week
Only listening during service
Practising every skill at once until it feels easy
practice.explanation: Short, frequent sessions work better than long, rare ones, and training one skill at a time keeps it manageable.

practice.question: You play a C major chord, then a single G. What number is the G?
practice.explanation: Count up the C major scale: C (1), D (2), E (3), F (4), G (5). The 5 sounds stable but open.

videos.title: Music theory for dum-dums, full beginner course (Piano With Corey)

practice.question: You get a voice note of a song you need for Sunday. What should you work out first?
options: The exact voicing of every chord
The lyrics of the bridge
The key note: where the song rests
The drum pattern
practice.explanation: Everything else depends on the key. Once you know the 1, you can turn every bass note into a number.

practice.question: Why follow the bass line to find the chords?
options: The bass usually plays each chord's root
The bass always plays the melody
The bass is always in the key of C
The bass never changes notes
practice.explanation: The lowest note usually tells you the root of each chord. Turn those roots into numbers and you have the progression.

practice.question: The song is in E. The bass goes E, C#, A, B. What are the numbers?
practice.explanation: E major is E F# G# A B C# D#. E = 1, C# = 6, A = 4, B = 5: 1-6-4-5, likely E C#m A B.

project.title: Learn a song by theory
checklist: Chose a song I have not played before
Wrote the time signature and tempo
Wrote every section in numbers, with the section order
Wrote the chord names in the original key under the numbers
Noted any sevenths, borrowed chords or key changes
Played the chart along with the recording and fixed mistakes
Recorded myself playing the song from my chart alone
